articles.title: Russia Preparing New Mobilization Wave of 600,000, Ukrainian Intelligence Says
articles.body:
Ukrainian intelligence data indicates that Russia is preparing plans for an additional wave of mobilization in 2026–2027, according to the Office of the President of Ukraine.
Russian authorities are reportedly planning to recruit 300,000 people this year and another 300,000 next year.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The report says the additional mobilization wave is a response by Russia’s political leadership to the loss of initiative in the war, steadily rising personnel losses on the front and a significant slowdown in contract recruitment across the regions.
“Russia’s personnel losses from January through July 2026 amounted to around 240,000 people, of whom at least 140,000 were irrecoverable. At the same time, fewer people – 232,000 – were recruited under contract into the Russian occupation contingent during this period,” the presidential office said.
How many people and whom Russia plans to mobilize
Ukraine says the Russian General Staff has already prepared a plan for the additional mobilization of 600,000 people over specified periods this year and next.
“As part of preparations for the additional mobilization wave and the recruitment of criminal elements under contract, the process of amending Russian legislation and regulations has begun. Control over military registration is being significantly tightened, mechanisms are being created to recruit people serving sentences in Russia’s prisons and penal colonies, and additional coercive measures are being developed,” Ukraine’s military intelligence agency said.
CIA Chief Warned Putin Against NATO Attack During Surprise Moscow Visit – Reports
The categories of convicted people eligible for military service have been expanded to include people with outstanding or unexpunged convictions under 11 articles of Russia’s Criminal Code.
These include crimes involving the smuggling of poisonous, radioactive and explosive substances, weapons and narcotics; banditry and organizing or participating in criminal groups; organizing illegal migration; violations of safety requirements at fuel and energy facilities; and the illegal handling, theft or extortion of nuclear materials or radioactive substances, among other offenses.
The Russian leadership has also approved extending mobilization and/or contract recruitment to significant categories of women serving sentences in prisons and penal colonies.
Work is also underway to establish recruitment quotas for law enforcement agencies, including the Interior Ministry, Federal Bailiffs Service, Federal Penitentiary Service and Investigative Committee, to send employees for military service under mobilization.
How long will mobilized troops be trained?
Depending on their level of training and the anticipated “survival” period of those mobilized by Russia, training could last between 15 and 60 days.
Some mobilized personnel could also be trained at military ranges in Belarus, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
The Russian leadership is preparing a package of measures to respond to potential negative social and economic consequences of placing cities and regions under a stricter wartime regime.
Internal Russian documents reportedly justify the need for an additional mobilization wave by pointing to a significant increase in regional dissatisfaction with the war, with dissatisfaction levels reaching as high as 69%, and a corresponding decline in the number of people willing to voluntarily sign military contracts.
Where is Russia struggling most to recruit?
Recruitment problems are reportedly most pronounced in the Oryol and Vladimir regions, as well as in Dagestan.
In the Kurgan region, monthly recruitment targets have been only 57–69% fulfilled since the beginning of the year. In the Volgograd region, the number of potential contract recruits has fallen by 40% compared with 2025.
Similar declines are being recorded in many other Russian regions.
Compared with 2025, some regions have seen a 30–40% drop in the number of debtors, convicted prisoners and other criminal elements, migrants and other groups that had long served as a key pool of contract recruits for the Russian military and its war against Ukraine.
A campaign to recruit students has also failed, despite involving the overwhelming majority of Russian universities.
How the Kremlin plans to enforce mobilization
The Russian leadership also plans to increase the personal responsibility of regional authorities and expand the powers of law enforcement agencies.
Russia has already introduced a system for issuing electronic mobilization notices. Authorities are developing additional coercive measures, including bans on leaving Russia, taking out loans, buying or selling real estate, revoking driving licenses and blocking funds in bank accounts.
Businesses are also expanding their military registration and mobilization departments. As of the end of July 2026, more than 2,500 new vacancies had been posted on Russian employment platforms for positions in these mobilization units, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
The most likely scenario is that Russian President Vladimir Putin will make a decision on mobilization after Russia’s State Duma “elections,” scheduled for Sept. 18–20 this year.

articles.title: CIA Chief Warned Putin Against NATO Attack During Surprise Moscow Visit – Reports
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow on Tuesday to warn Russian President Vladimir Putin against attacking a NATO member, amid the Kremlin’s stalled war against Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal and Politico reported on Wednesday, Aug. 26, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The warnings reportedly focused on Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania – the three Baltic NATO members that border Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The US intelligence community has previously assessed that Moscow could seek to “test NATO’s resolve” with a limited attack on an alliance member, according to the WSJ. US officials reportedly believe such an attack could involve a cyberattack or a small-scale ground incursion into one of the Baltic states.
The assessment comes as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to consume Western ammunition stocks, potentially creating vulnerabilities that Moscow could seek to exploit, according to WSJ sources.
Ratcliffe also warned Putin against providing military and economic support to Iran, Politico reported.
Neither Washington nor Moscow has publicly disclosed the results of Ratcliffe’s visit.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin did not meet with Ratcliffe and that the CIA chief’s contacts in Moscow were conducted at the intelligence-services level.
US President Donald Trump described the trip as “semi-routine.”
Did CIA Chief Warn Moscow Against NATO Attack – or Discuss Iran-Russia Ties?
After returning to Washington, however, Ratcliffe attended a closed-door meeting between Trump and senior US national security officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The meeting lasted about three hours.
Ratcliffe’s visit echoes a similar trip by then-CIA Director William Burns to Moscow in November 2021, just months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Burns met with senior Russian officials, including then-Security Council Secretary Nikolai Patrushev and Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin. He also spoke with Putin by phone.
According to CNN, Burns warned Moscow about the consequences of its troop movements near Ukraine and stressed that an invasion would be unacceptable.
Putin ultimately launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Washington asked Kyiv to hold fire
Ahead of Ratcliffe’s trip, Washington asked Ukraine to temporarily suspend strikes on Russian territory while the US delegation was in Moscow.
Axios reported that the US told Kyiv a senior delegation was traveling to Moscow and asked Ukraine to pause strikes until it had left.
Ukrainian government sources later confirmed to public broadcaster Suspilne that Washington specifically asked Kyiv not to strike Moscow and St. Petersburg during the visit.
The request came as Ukrainian forces have increasingly carried out long-range strikes against targets deep inside Russia, including in the Moscow region.

articles.title: Russia plans to mobilize additional 300,000 in 2026, 300,000 in 2027 - HUR, SZR

Russia is working on plans for an additional wave of mobilization in 2026-2027, aiming to recruit 300,000 people this year and 300,000 next year, according to a joint statement by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) and Foreign Intelligence Service (SZR), published on the Presidential Office’s website on Thursday.
"Russia’s political leadership views carrying out an additional wave of mobilization as a response to the aggressor state’s loss of the initiative in the war, the steady rise in personnel losses at the front, and a noticeable slowdown in the recruitment of contract soldiers in the regions. This is confirmed by Ukrainian intelligence data. Russia’s personnel losses in January-July 2026 amounted to about 240,000, of which at least 140,000 were irrecoverable. At the same time, fewer people were recruited into the Russian occupation contingent on contract during this period - 232,000," the statement said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the aggressor state primarily plans to bring up to strength units and military formations fighting against Ukrainians, as well as Russian military units currently being formed.
The statement said a system for issuing electronic mobilization summonses has already been introduced, and an expansion of coercive measures is being developed: bans on leaving Russia, taking out loans, buying or selling real estate, revoking driver’s licenses, freezing bank account funds, and so on. Enterprises are expanding departments handling mobilization work and military registration. As of the end of July 2026, more than 2,500 new job postings had already been recorded on employment platforms for staffing these enterprise mobilization units.
"Most likely, Russia’s leader will make the decision on mobilization after the ‘elections’ to Russia’s State Duma, scheduled for Sept. 18-20 this year," the statement said.
According to HUR and SZR, an additional wave of mobilization and the recruitment of criminal elements on contracts is being prepared, mechanisms for additional recruitment of people serving sentences in Russia’s prison and camp system are being created, and additional coercive measures are being developed. The categories of convicts to be recruited into military service in the occupation contingent have been expanded to include those with outstanding or unexpunged convictions under 11 articles of Russia’s Criminal Code, including smuggling of poisonous, radioactive and explosive substances, weapons and drugs; banditry and organizing or participating in a criminal group (gang); organizing illegal migration; violating safety requirements at fuel and energy sector facilities; and illegal handling, theft or extortion of nuclear materials or radioactive substances.
Russia’s leadership has also approved extending mobilization and contract recruitment to certain numerically significant categories of women serving sentences in prisons and camps. Preparations are also underway to determine quotas for law enforcement agencies to send personnel for mobilized service.
Training some of the mobilized troops at training grounds in Belarus has not been ruled out.
In addition, Russia’s leadership is preparing a set of forceful response measures for possible negative social and economic consequences of shifting cities and regions to a stricter wartime regime, and plans to increase regional authorities’ personal accountability and expand law enforcement agencies’ powers. Mobilization is planned to be carried out against a backdrop of growing dissatisfaction with the war inside Russia itself.
"Internal Russian documents justify the need for an additional wave of mobilization by citing a significant rise in dissatisfaction with the war in the regions (dissatisfaction levels reaching as high as 69%) and a corresponding decline in people willing to sign contracts voluntarily. Contract recruitment problems are most pronounced in the Oryol and Vladimir regions, as well as in Dagestan. In the Kurgan region, monthly plans have been fulfilled at only 57-69% since the start of this year. In the Volgograd region, the number of potential contract recruits has fallen 40% compared with 2025. A trend toward further declines is being recorded in many other Russian regions as well. Compared with 2025, the number of debtors, special-status individuals among convicts and criminal elements, migrants and other categories that had long served as the main recruitment base for service in the Russian army and participation in the war has fallen by 30-40% in some regions. A student recruitment campaign, in which the overwhelming majority of Russian universities took part, has failed," HUR and SZR said.
As reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is convinced Russia will carry out a new wave of mobilization for the war against Ukraine after its election campaign this fall. "We believe it won’t be in the major cities. But I don’t think they’ll be able to hide it very well. Their plan is for this to be a kind of peripheral mobilization," he said.
As for where Russia might send the mobilized troops, the president believes it will primarily be toward Kostiantynivka and Sloviansk (Donetsk region).
On Aug. 24, the president said Ukraine will no longer let Russia seize the initiative and will be ready for the mobilization planned in the aggressor state. "Russia doesn’t want peace - it wants mobilization. Well, we’re taking that in with a cool head. We’re acting. We need to strengthen our military and have everything we need to hold the defense. Our soldiers must be provided and equipped with everything, so that reinforcements for the enemy army turn into fertilizer for our land," Zelenskyy said in his Independence Day address to the citizens of Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian Aerospace Forces Received New Batch of at Least Two Su-35S Fighters
articles.body:
The Russian Aerospace Forces have received a new batch of Su-35S fighters.
Photos and videos of the handover were published by the United Aircraft Corporation, a subsidiary of Rostec.
The footage shows at least two new fighter jets.
The Su-35 is a Russian 4++-generation multi-role all-weather fighter jet.
To engage air and ground targets, the aircraft uses R-77, R-73, and Kh-31 missiles, guided bombs, and a 30-mm GSh-30-1 automatic cannon. The main component of its onboard avionics is the “Irbis-E” radar system with a passive phased-array antenna, capable of detecting targets at long ranges.
Russia uses the Su-35 primarily to provide cover for strike groups of Su-34 fighter-bombers, to intercept Ukrainian UAVs and cruise missiles, and to counter Ukrainian air defense systems.
As a reminder, the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine released data on 79 companies involved in the production of Russian Su-35S aircraft.
Twenty-two companies on this list are not yet subject to sanctions from any of the countries in the sanctions coalition.

articles.title: Patriot missile shortage in Europe reaches 'beyond critical' level — media
articles.body:
NEW YORK, August 27. /TASS/. The US military is experiencing a "beyond critical" shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe, particularly for Patriot systems, raising concerns about NATO countries’ vulnerability, The Associated Press reported, citing sources.
According to a US official, the most serious shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors capable of shooting down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. A NATO official confirmed low Patriot inventories among American and NATO forces in Europe.
The American military in Europe "definitely" does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have "very limited" capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray missile that goes off course, the US official said.
The agency linked the situation primarily to the transfer of US missile stocks from Europe to the Middle East amid the US war with Iran. There, US and allied forces have fired significant numbers of interceptors, including Patriot missiles, to repel Iranian drone and missile attacks.

articles.title: Did CIA Chief Warn Moscow Against NATO Attack – or Discuss Iran-Russia Ties?
articles.body:
US Senator Richard Blumenthal said Wednesday he hopes CIA Director John Ratcliffe used his rare visit to Moscow to deliver a blunt warning to Russian President Vladimir Putin against any further escalation, as questions continue to surround the purpose of the unannounced trip.
“My hope is that he delivered a warning about escalation, namely forget about it. There will be consequences,” Blumenthal told a press conference in Kyiv on Wednesday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Democratic senator stressed that he had no inside information about Ratcliffe’s mission but said Putin needed to understand that Washington would respond if Moscow pursued the kind of escalation US officials fear he may be considering.
“I’m very hopeful that the message was: ‘Don’t do it, forget about it. You’ll have no free shot,’” Blumenthal said.
Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday in one of the highest-level visits by a US official to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The trip was not announced in advance, fueling speculation about its purpose at a time when Russian attacks on Ukraine have intensified and US-brokered efforts to end the war have stalled.
US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the significance of the mission Wednesday, describing Ratcliffe’s trip as “semi-routine” while suggesting it was connected to efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
France Warns of New Hybrid Threat After Leipzig Drone Attack
“He’s there, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump told conservative radio host Glenn Beck.
Trump dismissed suggestions that Ratcliffe had traveled to Moscow specifically to warn Russia against testing NATO’s resolve or to discuss Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.
“Something may come out” of the visit, Trump said, adding that his administration was working to bring the war to an end.
“We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point,” Trump said.
The Kremlin confirmed Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials but said he did not meet Putin.
“There were contacts through the intelligence agencies, but there were no meetings of any kind with the Russian president,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, according to AFP.
Peskov said Putin had been briefed on the talks afterward but declined to reveal whether Ukraine was discussed or what messages Ratcliffe had delivered.
He described the resumption of contacts between US and Russian intelligence services as positive but cautioned against assuming the meeting would lead to an improvement in relations between Washington and Moscow.
“Contacts through the intelligence services are a positive development in and of themselves,” Peskov said.
Ratcliffe’s trip came amid growing concern over the possibility of further Russian escalation. Ukrainska Pravda reported that US intelligence had detected signs Russia could be making early preparations for a possible military mobilization.
Washington also reportedly asked Kyiv to temporarily suspend attacks on Moscow and St. Petersburg while Ratcliffe was in the Russian capital.
Trump, however, publicly rejected speculation that the CIA director’s trip was primarily intended to address a potential Russian move against NATO, telling Beck that reports describing such a purpose were incorrect.
NATO warning dominates speculation, while Iran angle draws less attention
The most widely reported explanation for Ratcliffe’s trip is that he went to Moscow to warn Russia against attacking or testing NATO. The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Ratcliffe’s mission was to deliver such a warning amid US intelligence assessments that Moscow could be considering provocative action against NATO members.
That theory has been reinforced by two factors. First, Ratcliffe’s visit closely echoes then-CIA Director William Burns’ November 2021 trip to Moscow, undertaken at President Joe Biden’s direction to warn Putin and other senior Russian officials against invading Ukraine and outline the consequences. Russia launched its full-scale invasion only months later.
Second, US intelligence agencies warned earlier this month that Putin could be increasingly willing to test NATO’s resolve through provocations, including hybrid operations, cyberattacks or other deniable actions falling short of a conventional military assault.
A less-discussed possibility is that Ratcliffe’s visit involved Russia’s growing support for Iran. Moscow has provided Tehran with intelligence on US military assets in the Middle East, while Russia and Iran have expanded cooperation involving satellite imagery and drone technology.
The issue has already surfaced in US-Russia contacts this year. In March, Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev reportedly proposed that Moscow stop providing Iran with intelligence on US military targets if Washington ended intelligence support for Ukraine. The proposal, delivered during talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, was reportedly rejected by Washington. The Kremlin later denied that such an offer had been made.
Ratcliffe is the first known CIA director to travel to Moscow since William Burns visited in November 2021.
The CIA has maintained limited channels with its Russian counterparts during the war, including contacts related to prisoner exchanges and efforts to prevent direct escalation between Moscow and Washington.

articles.title: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory, deputy defence minister says
articles.body:
Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory, deputy defence minister says
BRUSSELS, Aug 27 - Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory, Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski said on Thursday.
"No — that is what I would like to say very clearly and openly. Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory," Zalewski told reporters when asked whether future U.S. military presence in Poland could include nuclear capability.
"We want to participate in NATO nuclear deterrence, which does not mean having nuclear warheads on our territory," Zalewski said at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
He added that Poland was interested in increasing the permanent U.S. military presence under Washington's Force Posture Review and referenced U.S. President Donald Trump's remarks earlier this year on the possibility of sending additional troops to Poland.
Washington announced a six-month review of U.S. troop deployments in Europe in June. According to a document seen by Reuters it will create at least four sets of options for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth by November 6, well ahead of a December deadline.
"We treat President Trump's decision as a tool to improve European security, aligned with the Pentagon's concept of NATO 3.0. It means that it's due to Europeans to defend conventionally, but the U.S. maintains an extremely important role to support European armed forces," he said.
"Of course the starting point is a message sent to the public opinion by President Trump about sending 5,000 American soldiers to Poland on a permanent basis," he added.
In May, Trump surprised NATO allies by pledging to send an additional 5,000 troops to Poland. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia says it could strike UK military targets in response to Kyiv's use of British missiles
articles.body:
Russia says it could strike UK military targets in response to Kyiv's use of British missiles
MOSCOW, Aug 27 - Russia warned on Thursday that it could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukrainian attacks on targets inside Russia using long-range British cruise missiles.
The warning, delivered by Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova at a news briefing in Moscow, has been made before but without such rhetorical force or urgency.
Zakharova said that London was just "one step away" from becoming legally complicit — in Moscow's eyes — for what she called "terrorism" against Russian civilians and warned of "inevitable catastrophic consequences" unless Britain changed course.
Her reference to "terrorism" was related to the use of the Franco-British Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles by Ukraine to strike targets inside Russia or targets on territory in eastern Ukraine, which Russia claims as its own.
"We have repeatedly warned that any British military installations and equipment in Ukraine and beyond its borders could be targeted in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory carried out using British weapons," said Zakharova.
"We propose that the British leadership once again carefully analyse the situation and immediately, in the most resolute and unequivocal manner, abandon the hostile, aggressive line, which can only ... create the risk of the conflict escalating to an entirely new level," she said.
There was no immediate response from London, which has previously brushed off similar Russian warnings and made it clear it is committed to doing whatever it thinks is necessary to help Ukraine defend itself against Russia.
Western analysts said the strength of the warning reflected Russian fury over Britain's decision — made public on Monday — to allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia.
The Kremlin said on Monday that Britain was methodically adding "fuel to the fire" after the announcement.
'DANGEROUS PATH'
France has already given its assent to license the technology for the European missile and Zakharova on Thursday also appeared to threaten Paris too.
She said that France and Britain were both "playing with fire" by supplying sensitive missile technology to Ukraine, something she said could have unpredictable consequences.
She also took aim at British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, saying he seemed to think he had a mandate for escalation and had chosen the most dangerous path when it came to Ukraine.
Zakharova issued her warning a day after Russia accused Ukraine of firing British Storm Shadow missiles at a shopping centre in the Russian-controlled city of Donetsk in eastern Ukraine in an attack it said wounded civilians, including children.
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine and Reuters could not independently verify the details of the attack.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians. Thousands of civilians have been killed since Russia sent its troops into Ukraine in 2022.
Far more Ukrainian civilians have been killed than Russian ones — according to U.N. data — but Kyiv has escalated its campaign against targets inside Russia this year and the Conflict Intelligence Team, an independent group that tracks the war, estimates that a total of 327 civilians were killed inside Russia in the first seven months of the year, the highest recorded rate since the war began. REUTERS

articles.title: Trump Dismisses Fears of Russian Strike On NATO After CIA Chief Visits Moscow
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump told reporters that he does not believe Moscow will attack a NATO nation amid rising concerns that Russian President Vladimir Putin will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test the Western alliance’s resolve.
Trump on August 27 told reporters in the Oval Office that he had engaged in "good talks" with Putin and that "he's not going to be attacking a NATO territory." He did not specify when those talks were held.
"I am not concerned...at all. There is no problem," Trump was quoted earlier as saying by news publication Axios when asked about a possible Russian provocation against a NATO state.
The remarks come as the Kremlin at the same time dismissed as "scare stories" reports in the US media suggesting Moscow could attack NATO and following a surprise visit by the CIA director to Moscow.
NATO Article 5 Assurances
Western European security has long been tied to NATO's mutual defense clause, Article 5, which states that an attack on one member nation constitutes an attack on all.
Many Western leaders and officials have expressed concerns over Trump's commitment to the military alliance. Trump has at times put into question a possible US response to an attack on a member state, while at other times reaffirming support for NATO.
A letter seen by RFE/RL reveals growing concern about Russian aggression in the Baltic states, speaking of a "deteriorating security environment" amid an "increased frequency of airspace violations and drone incursions."
The letter was sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and signed by the three Baltic European commissioners, Kaja Kallas, Andrius Kubilius, and Valdis Dombrovskis, as well as the Polish and Finnish commissioners.
Dated July 30, the letter was one of a series of alarm bells sounded about Russian aggression over the course of the summer that culminated in CIA Director John Ratcliffe's surprise visit to Moscow on August 25.
Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to urge the Kremlin against escalating with US allies -- particularly Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania -- sources briefed about the visit confirmed to RFE/RL on August 26.
'Every Six Months'
Axios quoted Trump as denying Ratcliffe had issued such a warning to the Russians.
"Ratcliffe sees his Russian counterpart once every six months or once every year. They have a very good relationship. There was no message and there was nothing unusual," Trump said.
But when asked about the matter later by reporters in the Oval Office, Trump appeared to back off, saying: "I don't want to comment on that, but they're not going to attack [NATO]."
The New York Times, citing current and former officials, said Ratcliffe gave his counterpart a bleak assessment of the state of the Russia's war against Ukraine and to urge the Kremlin to reach a deal before its military and economic situation becomes worse.
The Wall Street Journal earlier cited US intelligence as stating Russia may test NATO resolve with a limited incursion as early as this fall.
Baltic diplomats who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity confirmed there was additional intelligence during the summer of Russian false-flag operations but no indication about an imminent conventional attack.
They were also keen to point out that such operations might not be limited to the Baltics, a concern reinforced by recent cases of alleged or suspected Russian involvement in assassination attempts, fires, and drone incursions in several NATO countries, including Germany, Poland, and Slovakia.
NATO Members Pressed
Separately, a senior Pentagon official on August 27 pressed NATO allies to outline how they were answering US demands that they take more responsibility for Europe's defense as Washington reviews its force levels on the continent.
The US administration under Trump has ignited fears among allies that the US could cut back its forces in Europe following a six-month review that began in July.
"The spirit that we come in is obviously one...of consultation, of engagement. We want to hear from our allies," US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said during a visit for talks at NATO's headquarters in Brussels.
Washington has sent out a questionnaire asking European countries to explain their efforts in taking the forefront in protecting the continent.
"We're actually having a kind of down-to-business conversation about how we go forward together in a world in which Europe, which is obviously a very wealthy continent, can and is taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defense," Colby said.

articles.title: Belarus Started Building a Railroad for Military Facilities Near the Borders of the Kyiv and Chernihiv Regions
articles.body:
Belarus is building railway infrastructure for military facilities on the border with Ukraine, specifically near the Kyiv and Chernihiv regions.
The opposition website Belarusian Railway Workers’ Community reported this.
The training ground is being built in a forested area of the Rechitsa District near the Yakimaŭka station. This is a Class V intermediate station on the Kalinkovichi–Gomel section of the Gomel Branch of the Belarusian Railways (NOD-4). From the Kalinkovichi side, the station is connected to the single-track Yakimaŭka–Seno Zavod section. On the Gomel side, there is a double-track section between Yakimaŭka and Pribor. The station’s track layout includes two main tracks and two siding tracks, as well as two low passenger platforms.
The railway portion has been designated as the third phase of construction. It includes the track, loading and unloading facilities, electrical centralization and communication systems, outdoor lighting, and other systems for servicing railcars on the testing ground.
The third phase covers the entire railway service scheme: connection to the existing station track, placement of railcars on the depot grounds, organization of shunting operations, communications, and loading and unloading operations. Once this work is complete, the depot will be able to receive railcars directly from the BZhD network as a separate freight terminal.
The Gomel-based publication Flagshtok previously reported on the construction site and work progress in January. It established that the training ground is being built near the Yakimaŭka station and confirmed that work had begun. In July, satellite images showed a clearing for the future railway branch line, and in August, selected pages of technical documentation were made public, confirming the facility’s location near the station.
Based on a report by Oleg Lugovskiy, Head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on June 25 the completion of road infrastructure construction, as well as the construction of ammunition and fuel-lubricant storage facilities along the Ukrainian-Belarusian state border.
Earlier reports also point to the facility’s military purpose. The State Institution Capital Construction Directorate of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Belarus is listed as the client for the 2023 engineering and topographic foundation. The current set of documents already specifies the State Unitary Enterprise Voenproekt Institute—the documents pertain to various stages of project preparation.
Once the railway section is operational, the training ground will become a reception point for military trains heading toward Ukraine. A 60-car track, its own loading and unloading area, communications, and a centralized route from the station will significantly expand the ability to deploy, supply, and rotate units. The infrastructure is suitable for transporting personnel, weapons and military equipment, fuel, ammunition, engineering supplies, and other cargo; however, the project does not specify the exact types of cargo to be transported in the future.
The actual intensity of operations will become apparent once the facility is put into service. This will be evidenced by the inclusion of Track No. 3a and new turnouts in the station’s operational documents, the launch of communication systems, the approval of local operating procedures, and the first actual train movements. For now, the documentation reveals only the planned capabilities. The scope of work and the range of technical equipment indicate that the facility is designed for long-term operation.
The dedicated railway infrastructure will connect several military facilities, including a training ground in the Gomel Region. The client is RUP Institute ‘Voenproekt’, and TransSoyuzProekt LLC developed the project documentation.
The railway also includes a logistics center on the territory of the former Krichev-6 airbase, a facility on the territory of the 1405th Artillery Ammunition Depot (military unit 42707) near the village of Velyka Horozha in the Osipovichi District, which is the home base of Oreshnik, dispatched by the 4th State Central Inter-Service Training Ground of the Russian Ministry of Defense, also known as the Kapustin Yar training ground, military unit 15644.
Beltrans, together with its subsidiary BTLS-Moscow and the Belarusian Ministry of Defense, provided logistical support for the Russian army’s deployment during the invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

articles.title: Russia Used the 9M723-2 Iskander-1000 Missile Against Kyiv for the First Time
articles.body:
Russia used the upgraded 9M723-2 ballistic missile, codenamed Iskander-1000, for the first time. It was deployed during one of the combined missile strikes on Kyiv this summer.
The Defense Intelligence of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense reported this, publishing new data on the Russian ballistic missile on the War&Sanctions portal.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the 9M723-2 is part of the Russian Bora-M missile system.
The new missile differs from the base 9M723-1 model in that it has a larger engine, which has increased its range. The 9M723-2 is capable of striking targets at distances of up to 550 km, while the 9M723-1 has a range of approximately 390 km.
The Telegram channel Colonel GSh showed debris from this missile, with the marking Ts.M. 9M723-2 visible.
To accommodate the larger missile, the Russians also had to enlarge the launchers; however, according to the Defense Intelligence (DIU), the rest of the missile’s components remained identical to those of the 9M723-1.
Militarnyi reported on the possible emergence of this missile a year ago. At that time, a relatively small order for 18 9M723-2 missiles was discovered in the contracts of Russia’s Machine-Building Design Bureau, with production planned for 2025.
At that time, it was speculated that the 9M723-2 might be linked to the Iskander-1000 extended-range missile project. The contract price for a single missile was estimated at RUB 221 million, or about $2.5 million.
The 9M723 is the primary ballistic missile of Russia’s Iskander-M SRBM. It can carry a warhead weighing about 500 kg.
According to Militarnyi, Russia’s Machine-Building Design Bureau received an order for 1,202 ballistic missiles of various 9M723 modifications for the 2024–2025 period. Of these, 589 missiles were scheduled for manufacture in 2024, and another 643 in 2025.
The largest portion of the order was for the 9M723-1F2 missile with a fragmentation-high-explosive warhead—771 units. Another 217 missiles were designated 9M723-1F3, 185 were 9M723-1K5 with a cluster warhead, and 59 were 9M723-1F1.
Thus, the first deployment of the 9M723-2 confirms that Russia not only ordered this low-production variant but also brought it into combat use.

articles.title: China’s Xi Jinping to visit Egypt for first time in a decade
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
China’s Xi Jinping to visit Egypt for first time in over a decade
Chinese President Xi Jinping will visit Egypt in the coming days – his first trip to the country since 2016, as Beijing and Cairo pursue deeper trade, security and technology ties amid regional instability and surveillance concerns.
The stay, expected to last from 30 August to 3 September, will follow Xi’s attendance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
Xi is set to meet Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi for talks that Beijing says will contribute to "safeguarding peace and stability in the region". China’s foreign ministry said the state visit holds "special significance" for bilateral ties, while Egypt’s presidency said the leaders will discuss their strategic partnership and regional and international issues.
The trip coincides with 70 years of diplomatic relations, with Egypt being the first Arab country to establish formal relations with the People’s Republic of China in 1956. Sisi last travelled to Beijing in May 2024, where both sides agreed a three-year action plan covering trade, technology, security and climate change.
Trade and investment
China has become one of Egypt’s main commercial partners, although the relationship remains heavily imbalanced.
Bilateral trade reached around $20.8bn in 2025, according to Egypt’s Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, up from $17.38bn in 2024. Egyptian exports to China are estimated at $2bn–$3bn, while Chinese imports are valued at about $15bn–$16bn.
Cairo has sought to convert Chinese investment into manufacturing capacity and exports. This month, Egyptian and Chinese companies signed 17 export contracts worth about $168m, including agricultural, food, mineral and engineering products.
Chinese companies have expanded their presence in Ain Sokhna’s Suez Canal Economic Zone, where more than 200 firms now operate. Beijing views the zone as a manufacturing and logistics gateway to European, African and Middle Eastern markets, while Egypt hopes it will bring jobs, foreign currency and technology transfer.
The partnership has gained strategic weight during disruption to Middle Eastern energy and shipping routesdue to the US-Israel war with Iran that heavily impacted the key maritime corridor through the Strait of Hormuz. China depends heavily on the region for crude imports, while Egypt’s Suez Canal remains one of the most important links between Asian and European trade.
Military and technology cooperation
Security cooperation has also accelerated between the two countries. On 22 August, Egypt and China began the Eagles of Civilization 2026 air exercise, which includes training in planning and managing aerial combat.
Six Chinese J-16 fighter jets reportedly flew more than 6,000km in nine hours to take part, marking the first time the aircraft had reached Mediterranean Africa for an exercise. Analysts argue that the drills signal Beijing’s growing ability to project military power into North Africa and Egypt’s interest in broadening defence relationships beyond its traditional Western suppliers.
Huawei has meanwhile submitted a bid to supply Egyptian authorities with 1,408 top-end Ascend 950-series AI chips for an AI training and cloud computing system, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. The proposal includes another 600 chips for two inference clusters designed to run AI models.
Huawei says it could build the infrastructure within a year, where the reported plan would supply AI data centres for Egyptian military, surveillance and other government applications – potentially making Egypt an important regional platform for Huawei’s AI business.
Bloomberg reported that the US State Department contacted Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft after learning of Huawei’s pitch, seeking counter-offers and warning that unauthorised use of some AI accelerators could trigger legal sanctions.
Surveillance concerns
The reported proposal also involves iFlytek, a Chinese AI and surveillance company that offers facial and vehicle-recognition technology. Combined with a national population database and high-capacity AI computing, such a system could enable authorities to identify and track people at scale.
That raises serious rights concerns in Egypt, where authorities have been accused of closely monitoring journalists, activists, opposition figures and online critics. Human Rights Watch, among other rights groups, has pointed out how peaceful protests remain effectively banned and that authorities continue to target dissenting expression.
Egyptian digital rights groups have also recently opposed requirements for telecom users to submit facial images, fingerprints and other biometrics, warning that combining such records with state databases could enable broad profiling and surveillance.
iFlytek is likely to draw particular attention because the US Commerce Department placed it on an export blacklist in 2019 over allegations that its technology contributed to China’s repression and high-tech surveillance of Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities in Xinjiang. The company has denied wrongdoing.

articles.title: Ukraine downs 7 ballistic missiles, 1 Oniks missile, 3 Banderol drones and 222 Russian UAVs, but strikes recorded
articles.body:
Ukraine downs 7 ballistic missiles, 1 Oniks missile, 3 Banderol drones and 222 Russian UAVs, but strikes recorded
Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, two anti-ship missiles and 258 strike drones on the night of 26-27 August. Ukrainian air defence downed 233 Russian aerial assets.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force on Facebook
Details: The Air Force reported that Russia had launched two Oniks anti-ship missiles from temporarily occupied Crimea, Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk and Kursk oblasts and 258 Shahed attack UAVs (around a third of which were jet-powered), Gerbera drones, S8000 Banderol drones and Parodiya decoy drones.
The drones were launched from Kursk, Millerovo, Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia and temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea.
The main targets of the Russian attack were Odesa, Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
Ukrainian aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units as well as mobile fire groups have been involved in repelling the attack.
Early reports as of 09:00 indicated that Ukrainian air defence had shot down or jammed one Oniks anti-ship missile, seven Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, three S8000 Banderol drones and 222 Russian UAVs of various types in the south, north, east and centre of Ukraine.
Hits by Russian aerial weapons were recorded at 15 locations and debris from downed aerial assets landed at 11 locations.
The Air Force added that some Russian weapons have failed to reach their targets and that information concerning them is still being verified.
The Russian attack is still ongoing, as several UAVs remain in Ukrainian airspace.
Background:
- In summer 2026, Ukraine has been facing an acute shortage of anti-ballistic missiles for its air defence systems. The military leadership subsequently decided to restrict information in morning reports on the number of Russian ballistic missiles launched and destroyed during large-scale combined attacks.
- On 26 August, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that following recent meetings in the NB8 and Coalition of the Willing formats, Ukraine had received "a few missiles" for Patriot systems as well as AIM missiles, but stressed that more are needed.

articles.title: US Patriot missile shortage in Europe ‘beyond critical’ due to Iran war, officials say
articles.body:
US Patriot missile shortage in Europe ‘beyond critical’ due to Iran war, officials say
In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault, Nato could be forced ‘to take punch after punch in the mouth’
The US military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe largely driven by US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, an American defence official in Europe and a Nato official said, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in Nato countries to a potential Russian attack.
The US defence official said the most concerning shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles.
The Nato official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and Nato forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, Nato could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth”, the US defence official said.
In Europe, the American military “definitely” does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have “very limited” capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray Russian missile that goes off course, the US official said.
It illustrates the cascading fallout from Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran, a conflict that reaches the six-month mark on Friday.

articles.title: France is also not ready for the threat posed by cheap drones
articles.body:
The French Chief of the Defense Staff, General Fabien Mandon, warned on the 26th of August that the country is not yet ready to confront relatively cheap and mass-produced threats such as drones, writes Politico.
Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, financially sustainable defense against relatively cheap, mass-produced weapons, including the Iranian-made Shahed drones, has become one of the main challenges for Western militaries.
Mandon, at an event organized by France’s main business lobby, Medef, warned that there are enemies who have developed a large number of cheap solutions that can drain French defense resources. He said that this is not happening yet, there is no catastrophe, and the country is peaceful, but action must be taken.
NATO’s arsenal consists of sophisticated, high-tech missiles, each worth millions, that the army, navy and air force use to shoot down remotely piloted aircraft worth tens of thousands of dollars.
The main goal now is to reduce the so-called cost per kill — that is, to reduce the price of neutralizing a threat.
Recently, the French Air Force has used expensive missiles to shoot down cheap Iranian drones that it has been targeting in the Persian Gulf.
French arms manufacturers such as MBDA and start-ups including Alta Ares and Harmattan AI are working on cheaper, mass-produced weapons to counter the threat. Mandon said defensive weapons are not yet being produced in the quantities needed to stop intense waves of attacks. He added that he is working to accelerate the use of drones in the French armed forces. The general also noted that defense industry companies must be able to adapt to a rapidly changing world where competitors are adapting very quickly.

articles.title: CIA Director Warns Russia Against Attacking Baltic States — Politico
articles.body:
During his visit to Moscow, U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe warned Russia against attacking U.S. NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
Politico reported this, citing sources familiar with the trip details.
Ratcliffe also used his trip to the Russian capital on Tuesday to urge the country to reduce its military and economic support for Iran.
“The meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states,” one of the sources said.
In recent weeks, Russia has issued a series of threats against NATO countries supporting Ukraine. This has raised concerns that Moscow could resort to new hybrid or limited military actions against NATO members, including the United Kingdom.
On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump denied media reports suggesting that Ratcliffe made the trip to persuade Russia not to test NATO’s resolve or take aggressive action against the United Kingdom.
He described the visit as “semi-routine” but acknowledged that it also focused on ending the Russo-Ukrainian war.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow on Tuesday, August 25, aboard a C-17A Globemaster III military transport aircraft.
The aircraft landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport at 10:04 a.m.
Ratcliffe’s visit to Russia’s capital had not been announced in advance.
Financial Times journalist Christopher Miller previously reported that representatives of the Donald Trump administration had asked Kyiv last week not to strike Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other Russian regions on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday — the period when the U.S. was expected to send a top-ranking official to Russia. According to Miller, Ukraine agreed to the request.
This was Ratcliffe’s first visit to Russia since becoming CIA director and one of the highest-level contacts between the Trump administration and Moscow in recent months.

articles.title: A stab in the back: Why an AfD victory in Saxony could pose a national security threat to Germany
articles.body:
For the first time in its history, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has a real chance of forming a regional government. On Sept. 6, voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will go to the polls, and experts are already describing scenarios in which the AfD would have enough votes to govern alone. In that case, the German political system’s “firewall” — the voluntary commitment of other parties not to cooperate with the radical right — would prove powerless. The AfD’s rise to power even in a state as small and economically weak as Saxony-Anhalt could cause serious problems for Berlin — including in the key areas of defense and security.
The “plan for Germany” is under threat
In Germany, a regional government cannot directly influence the nation’s foreign or defense policy. This is the exclusive prerogative of the federal center, in the form of the Bundestag and the government. That said, the AfD makes no secret of its opposition to weapons deliveries to Ukraine and to broader European rearmament plans. The party describes Berlin’s actions as a “course toward war” and demands “the restoration of partnership with Russia.”
Even if a party representative were to take the premier’s seat in Magdeburg, they would be unable to change Germany’s current geopolitical course. Moreover, the authors of Germany’s Basic Law anticipated the possibility of conflict between the federal center and a state, embedding protective mechanisms in two separate articles.
Article 37 allows the federal government to apply coercive measures in the event that local authorities refuse to follow a national decision. Additionally under Article 85, the federal government may issue direct instructions to the states within the framework of so-called “federal supervision.” But the process isn’t simple.
If an event in Europe were to trigger NATO’s Article 5 mechanism, Germany’s civilian authorities and military would begin implementing the Operational Plan for Germany (OPLAN DEU) — a set of mobilization and logistics measures that include the redeployment of large military contingents and equipment from western and southern Europe to the east, and Berlin’s allies would be counting on the use of German territory as a key hub for defensive operations. Although the exact routes for convoy movements are classified, several factors suggest that Saxony-Anhalt has been assigned an important role in such plans.
First, the geographic location of the state is perfect, as it sits halfway between the western part of the country and Poland. As a result, virtually the only route for a rapid response runs through Saxony-Anhalt. After all, numerous key Bundeswehr bases and logistics centers are located in and around the state.
Second, this region has in recent years undergone large-scale rehabilitation of its rail network, autobahns, and secondary roads. Many of them are now considered to be among the best in Germany. Plans through 2029 call for further modernization of the central rail hubs in Magdeburg and Dessau, as well as capacity expansion on the Magdeburg–Berlin route.
A state government, if it chooses, could significantly slow down military convoy movements at precisely the moment when every hour counts. For example, a hypothetical premier of Saxony-Anhalt who opposes “escalation” and calls for “seeking compromises at the negotiating table” could refuse to issue the permits required for heavy — and especially tracked — military vehicles to pass through the region, as the issuance of such permits falls within the competence of the relevant state authority. In addition, military convoys are required to move exclusively with a police escort whose purpose is to close off civilian traffic, and law enforcement agencies are subordinate to local authority.
A state government could significantly slow down military convoy movements at the very moment when every hour counts
Finally, decisions about the use of regional infrastructure — such as allocating land for tent camps and ensuring supplies of electricity, water, and fuel — are made locally, not at the federal center. Even the exchange of information between central command structures and the operations hub in Magdeburg could be significantly hampered.
There is no doubt that in an emergency, Berlin would immediately invoke its powers under the relevant articles of the Basic Law, and it is also fair to assume that not every senior police officer would agree to openly sabotage defensive measures. But precious hours — or even days — could still be lost, creating grave ramifications for the defensive strategy of both Germany individually and NATO as a whole.
Red tape as a weapon
The reputation of German bureaucracy is renowned far beyond the country’s borders. On one hand, the meticulous observance of the letter of the law and strict adherence to procedure guarantee a functioning rule-of-law state, reducing the actual power of those in positions of authority.
On the other hand, what makes the system stable simultaneously renders it vulnerable to legalistically legitimate, functionally pointless legal challenges. Although the AfD’s core political demands are unachievable without the approval of the Bundestag and the federal government, authorities at the state level possess all of the necessary mechanisms to make life considerably more difficult for the chancellor and their ruling coalition in Berlin.
A state is a significant player on Germany’s political field. The Bundesrat, the chamber of the states, approves nearly 40% of the laws passed by the Bundestag — and that approval is far from automatic. Since the Federal Republic’s founding in 1949, the Bundesrat veto has been used more than 100 times.
Moreover, some initiatives approved by the government and the upper house of parliament — such as recent payments to the public that required co-financing from the states — were never unblocked. And even though Saxony-Anhalt has only four of the Bundesrat’s 69 seats, this by no means implies legal weakness.
Presently, AfD parliamentary groups in the Bundestag and the state parliaments frequently pressure the executive and legislative branches with a barrage of motions, bills, and inquiries. These often lack any legal basis, but the system is obliged to respond to them.
For the AfD, this is an opportunity to demonstrate activity to its voters and convince them of its own effectiveness as the “only genuine opposition.” Moreover, around 7,000 AfD inquiries concerning the state of critical infrastructure and the country’s defense between 2020 and 2025 raise serious concerns among politicians and journalists.
Armed with votes in the Bundesrat and a new lever of influence, the AfD could well push this process to the point of absurdity, creating tangible stress for government administration. A state is what is known as a “constitutional body,” meaning it has the right to file a complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. Under the unwritten rules of the game, a state government hardly ever resorts to this instrument — only in cases where the state’s rights have been seriously violated and numerous mediation councils with the federal center have yielded no result.
Statistically, state lawsuits account for just 1% of all cases examined by the Constitutional Court, and referrals to the court to review the legality of a given federal law are almost as rare — in the range of two to three per year. However, there are no legal limitations on the number referrals that can be submitted, meaning that a state under AfD rule could well disregard the unwritten rules and flood the Constitutional Court with challenges to any law passed by the Bundestag. The focus would be, first and foremost, on the issues most sensitive to a radical electorate: the entry and residence of foreign nationals, refugee admissions, environmental policy, and funding for renewable energy development, gender equality programs, and measures to strengthen European unity.
A state under AfD rule could flood the Constitutional Court with challenges to any law passed by the Bundestag
Blocking tax legislation would also theoretically be possible, posing a potential threat to the smooth functioning of the country’s fiscal system. Admittedly, federal laws are not subject to suspensive effect — meaning their entry into force would not be suspended on account of a pending complaint. Still, a mass attack on the Constitutional Court would inevitably affect its productivity and, indirectly, the functioning of government bodies.
A state also has the right to file a so-called urgent application, which would indeed effectively block a law until a final decision is reached. As a rule, the Constitutional Court grants such an application only in exceptional cases of serious harm to the state and its residents, but here there is ample room for legal interpretation and hairsplitting.
Finally, while four seats in the Bundesrat represent a mere 3% of the total membership, even these could become a “golden share” under certain conditions. The AfD’s appearance in the Bundesrat as the ruling party in its state would further legitimize the far-right party, and in the event of a serious conflict between states or a deadlock in the body, one side might not be able to resist the temptation to form a temporary alliance with the AfD in order to secure victory in the dispute with the help of Saxony-Anhalt’s votes.
Reshaping the system
The intense focus of foreign — and indeed many German — observers exclusively on federal politics is understandable. The state level may seem dull and unimportant, but in Germany’s federalist model the region plays a significant role in the implementation of policy. The state commands numerous levers of government administration, and here, the AfD would obtain tangible opportunities to change a great deal if it were to come to power.
All school-level education, along with a significant share of higher education, is a state-level responsibility. In Germany, a teacher is not required to follow the textbook to the letter and enjoys considerable freedom in shaping lesson concepts, but a hypothetical AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt would be quite capable of reformatting the educational process.
The party’s attention is focused primarily on the subject of “history,” and it makes no secret of its rejection of the form of historical memory and perception of past events that has developed in the Federal Republic. Instead, it would prefer a departure from the sense of guilt — or more precisely, collective responsibility — of the German people for the crimes of Nazism, as well as from the negative assessment of the militarism of the Second Reich, the colonial period, and a number of historical figures from the last 150 years.
Ideally, the AfD wants to foster the development of German patriots who are proud of their country and do not dwell on the dark pages of its history. This approach could be reflected in new curricula, which teachers are not entitled to ignore.
The AfD wants to raise German patriots who are proud of their country and do not dwell on the dark pages of its history
The state Ministry of Education would also be able to exert sufficient administrative and financial pressure on schools and universities to shut down initiatives aimed at combating racism, xenophobia, homophobia, and sexism. The AfD has an extremely negative attitude toward gender equality and diversity, feminism, and the use of gender-neutral language, meaning all of these could become a thing of the past in the area under its authority.
Admittedly, under such a scenario, the human factor would play a considerable role. Would thousands of teachers, officials, and administrators be willing to comply with the new rules of the game? This is where the second important set of state-level powers comes into play: personnel policy. Saxony-Anhalt has approximately 115,000 public-sector employees — 12% of the entire working-age population — and in a region with high unemployment, low wages, and very poor prospects on the open labor market, some administrators may choose to adapt to the new realities rather than risk being dismissed. In the five years before the next elections, the AfD could well appoint “ideologically compatible” personnel to senior and mid-level positions. This also applies to the state Center for Political Education, an important government body promoting democracy, which the new government could restructure beyond recognition.
Finally, the state government controls the police and the Office for the Protection of the Constitution — the body that, back in November of 2023, classified the AfD’s state organization in Saxony-Anhalt as “definitively right-wing extremis.” Should the AfD come to power, it may be tempted to exact revenge on the agency. Meanwhile, the state police have already been mired in scandals on multiple occasions involving the discovery of racist and antisemitic messages in internal chats, while year after year, human rights activists record an increase in cases of police brutality.
Even worse, it is not inconceivable that some local police officers would welcome “a firm hand” in power. In addition, the state Interior Minister has the authority to block individual law enforcement operations, and a hypothetical AfD minister would undoubtedly make use of that privilege.
Not least, the emergence of an AfD-led government even at the state level would deal a crushing blow to the firewall. Germany’s Basic Law explicitly requires the states to cooperate with one another. Without this, German federalism would simply be unworkable. In practice, the regions are genuinely bound by political ties — from the Bundesrat, where the mode of cooperation is different from that in the neighboring chamber of parliament, to the format of joint conferences of relevant state ministers. Currently, such conferences are held in 21 areas — from meetings of state premiers to forums of interior, economics, justice and transport ministers.
The AfD’s rise to power in Saxony-Anhalt could provide the final contribution to the “normalization” of the far-right party on a wider scale.

articles.title: US deputy defence chief to visit NATO HQ, Patriot systems for Kyiv may be discussed
articles.body:
US deputy defence chief to visit NATO HQ, Patriot systems for Kyiv may be discussed
Elbridge Colby, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, is visiting NATO headquarters in Brussels on 27 August as part of US plans to review its military presence in Europe, according to sources. The issue of providing Ukraine with interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems may also be raised.
Source: European Pravda, citing sources in NATO and diplomatic circles
Details: The main topic of Colby's visit to NATO on 27 August is the US military presence in Europe, although military assistance to Ukraine may also come up during the discussions.
"The United States is holding consultations with allies as part of a review of the deployment and structure of its forces. The US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy will take part in a meeting of the North Atlantic Council tomorrow as part of these ongoing consultations," a NATO official told European Pravda's Brussels correspondent.
Sources in Brussels diplomatic circles also confirmed to European Pravda that the main purpose of the North Atlantic Council meeting on 27 August is to discuss the review of the deployment and structure of US forces in Europe.
Nevertheless, NATO diplomats said the issue of Ukraine could be raised during discussions with the US official.
European Pravda has also learned that another meeting of the North Atlantic Council at ambassadorial level took place on Wednesday 26 August, during which issues concerning Ukraine were among the topics discussed.
Participants at the meeting discussed the urgent need to provide Ukraine with more military assistance, particularly PAC-3 interceptor missiles and Patriot systems, which are currently among its most pressing needs.
Financial assistance to Ukraine was also discussed, including funding to cover the shortfall in the country's defence budget.
Background:
- Colby is visiting NATO headquarters in Brussels on 27 August.
- The US Department of Defense is currently reviewing its military presence in Europe, which could pave the way for a reduction in the number of US troops on the continent.
- CIA Director John Ratcliffe recently visited Moscow and, according to some reports, warned Russian officials against escalating tensions with US NATO allies, particularly Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

articles.title: Russia lashes out at UK, France over Ukraine missile technology transfer
articles.body:
Russia lashes out at UK, France over Ukraine missile technology transfer
Moscow warns of potential strikes on British military targets, urging London to change its stance on supporting Kyiv
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Thursday that Russia could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.
Zakharova called on Britain to back off what she called London’s hostile stance on Ukraine, which she said risked taking the conflict to an entirely new level.
She had told the same Moscow news briefing earlier that Britain and France were “playing with fire” by supplying sensitive missile technology to Ukraine.
Britain announced on Monday it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to licence the technology for the European missile.
Also on Thursday, the Kremlin dismissed US media reports that Russia could attack a Nato member state and that the purpose of US CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow this week had been to warn Russia against such a move.
Asked to comment on the reports, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said: “A lot of this kind of scare-story material is being published right now. Of course, it has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation.”

articles.title: The Kyiv region was attacked by Russian drones and ballistic missiles throughout the night; warehouses are on fire
articles.body:
The Kyiv region was attacked by Russian drones and ballistic missiles throughout the night; warehouses are on fire
Kyiv • UNN
Warehouses and private homes were damaged in the Kyiv region in the overnight attack. A fire broke out in Boryspil district; there are no casualties.
The Kyiv region was under attack by Russian drones and ballistic missiles all night; warehouses in two districts were damaged, and one caught fire, Kyiv Regional Military Administration Head Tymur Tkachenko reported on social media on Thursday, UNN writes.
Details
The enemy attacked the Kyiv region with strike drones and ballistic missiles throughout the night. In Boryspil district, the attack caused a fire in warehouse premises. articles.title: US orders more SM-3 IIA missile interceptors
articles.body:
Raytheon has received a $745 million contract to produce and sustain additional SM-3 Block IIA interceptors as the United States expands production capacity for ballistic missile defence weapons.
Raytheon has received a $745 million contract, approximately £553 million, from the US Missile Defense Agency for the production and sustainment of Standard Missile-3 Block IIA ballistic missile interceptors, according to the company.
The contract announced by RTX covers the SM-3 Block IIA, a missile developed cooperatively by Raytheon and Japanese industry. The interceptor is designed to defend against short- to intermediate-range ballistic missile threats and forms part of the wider Standard Missile family used for naval air and missile defence.
Compared with earlier SM-3 variants, the Block IIA incorporates a larger rocket motor and an enhanced kinetic warhead. Rather than relying on an explosive warhead to destroy an incoming ballistic missile, the interceptor’s kinetic element is intended to defeat the target through a high-speed collision. Raytheon says the larger design provides increased reach and allows a wider geographical area to be defended against ballistic missile threats.
Barbara Borgonovi, president of Naval Power at Raytheon, said, as quoted in a news update: “SM-3 Block IIA is a cornerstone of regional defense, giving the U.S. and allied partners greater reach, accuracy and confidence against evolving threats.”
She added: “We’ve made sustained investments in our production lines and processes, which are allowing us to increase capacity and deliver these critical munitions to our customers more quickly.”
The award comes as RTX expands manufacturing capacity across the Standard Missile programme. The company recently invested $115 million in its missile integration facility in Alabama, saying the expansion will increase integration and delivery capacity at the site by more than 50%.
Work under the latest contract will take place at Raytheon facilities in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama. RTX said it is also recruiting additional staff to support the programme as production capacity increases.

articles.title: Russia says it could strike UK military targets in response to Kyiv's use of British missiles
articles.body:
Russia says it could strike UK military targets in response to Kyiv's use of British missiles
MOSCOW, Aug 27 - Russia warned on Thursday that it could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukrainian attacks on targets inside Russia using long-range British cruise missiles.
The warning, delivered by Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova at a news briefing in Moscow, was the strongest of is kind yet from Russia to Britain, a NATO member state and a staunch ally of Ukraine.
Zakharova said London was "one step away" from becoming legally complicit in what she called "terrorism" against Russian civilians, something she said would have "catastrophic consequences" unless Britain changed course.
"We have repeatedly warned that any British military installations and equipment in Ukraine and beyond its borders could be targeted in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory carried out using British weapons," she said.
"We propose that the British leadership once again carefully analyse the situation and immediately, in the most resolute and unequivocal manner, abandon the hostile, aggressive line, which can only ... create the risk of the conflict escalating to an entirely new level," she said.
Zakharova issued her warning a day after Russia accused Ukraine of firing British Storm Shadow missiles at a shopping centre in the Russian-controlled city of Donetsk in eastern Ukraine in an attack which it said wounded civilians, including children.
The Kremlin said on Monday that Britain was methodically adding "fuel to the fire" after London announced it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to license the technology for the European missile. REUTERS

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.
The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.
“The stop is a routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.
Earlier this week, the Thai navy said that three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify the vessels or provide a date.
The planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeks amid reports of poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. The Navy Times also reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.
On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard told MS Now that her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.
Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which is defined as someone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.
The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” which is when the service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.
The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.
The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.
The navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. In a statement to MS Now about the decision to pursue a non-judicial punishment for the sailor, a navy official said that “the Navy is fully committed to the health and wellbeing of every Sailor”.
“We strive to foster environments that support mental health by removing barriers to seeking help, increasing awareness of resources, and taking appropriate action when someone is in need,” they added. “Mental health resources are available to our Sailors 24/7, and asking for help is a sign of strength.”
The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 November bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than 250 consecutive days without a significant port visit.
Reports about the conditions onboard have prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.
